## TL;DR

Task #1152 adds a one-action route from a connected server back to the native
RepoOS Hub server picker, and fixes the phone top bar so the current project
name is visible while search becomes a compact icon button. The connected
server runs in an isolated WebView with no Capacitor bridge, so I deliberately
did **not** add one. Instead, the shell opens each server with a fresh
`?repoos_hub=<token>` and watches its existing
`browserPageNavigationCompleted` event for an exact origin + return path +
token. The SPA's logo performs a full-page navigation to that landing path when
the token is present; the shell closes the WebView only on an exact match. In a
normal browser the token is absent, so the logo stays decorative and the desktop
top bar keeps its branch label and full search field. Focused tests cover the
contract, the native shell wiring, normal-browser behaviour and the
narrow-screen layout.

## Work and rationale

The biggest constraint was the existing security boundary. The native Hub opens
a user-supplied server with `@capacitor/inappbrowser`'s `openInWebView`, which
intentionally has no Capacitor bridge. Adding one just for a logo would give
every connected server native privileges and contradict
`docs/mobile-architecture.md`. I therefore treated "return to picker" as a
navigation handshake, which the plugin already supports.

The handshake lives in `src/core/hub-return.ts`, a small dependency-free module
shared by the native shell and the SPA. The shell creates a 128-bit token per
open, appends it with `withHubContext`, and keeps it in memory. The SPA reads it
with `readHubContext`, remembers it in `sessionStorage` so a login redirect can
return to it, and strips the query parameter from the visible URL. On logo
activation the SPA navigates to
`/__repoos_hub/return-to-picker#hub-return=<token>`; the fragment keeps the
token out of the server request. The shell accepts the navigation only when the
origin is exactly the one it opened, the path is exactly the return path, and
the fragment matches the current token. A stale token, a normal route or a
foreign origin is ordinary navigation.

The landing path is a tiny public, script-free page served by `serveHubReturn`
in `src/server/routes/ui.ts` and registered in `src/server/server.ts`. It lets
the WebView navigation complete immediately instead of booting the SPA, and
stays public so it still lands if the session expired while the WebView was
open. It has `no-store`, a restrictive CSP, and no scripts or data.

On the UI side, `src/ui-app/src/lib/hub-shell.ts` owns the browser half.
`claimHubContext()` runs once at boot before the router mounts, stores the
token, and removes it from the URL. `readHubShellSession()`, called by `TopBar`,
checks the URL first (login redirect) then the per-tab session token.
`returnToHubServerPicker()` performs a full `location.assign`, not a client-side
route, because only a document navigation produces the WebView event the shell
listens for. The shell wiring stays in `mobile/src/browser.ts`.

For the top bar, `TopBar.vue` renders the logo as a button only when a Hub
session exists; otherwise it keeps the decorative mark. The button has an
explicit accessible name and a 44x44 touch target on phones while the mark stays
visually 30px. `pillText` returns just the project name when
`useResponsiveLayout()` says the viewport is narrow, so a long branch cannot
crowd out the name; desktop keeps `repo × branch`. The chip's colour-picker
semantics are unchanged. Long names ellipsize inside a `min-width: 0` wrapper
and the branch glyph is hidden on phones.

`SearchBar.vue` gained an `aria-label`, and the phone breakpoint makes search a
fixed 44x44 icon button with its placeholder and `⌘K` chip hidden. That frees
the width the project chip now uses. I also hide the preview-build marker on
very narrow screens: it is developer chrome and would push the project name back
out. All colours come from existing theme variables, so light/dark and
alternate design themes are untouched.

## Approaches tried

I first considered a custom URL scheme (`repoos-hub://…`) or an injected
JavaScript interface. Both need native URL-scheme registration or a vendored
WebView wrapper, plus a new trust decision for every connected server. The
plugin already exposes the completed-navigation event, so the per-open token
handshake gave the same one-action UX without widening the native attack
surface. I kept the token in the URL fragment so the server never receives it.

I also considered making the logo a normal `<a>` everywhere, but that would
change desktop/browser behaviour for no benefit; the native-only button keeps
regressions out of the ordinary browser.

For the layout, the first pass simply removed the `display: none` on the pill
text. That left no room at 360–390px because the search pill was still flexing.
The final pass fixes search at 44px, lets the chip take the remainder, hides the
decorative branch icon, and ellipsizes the name.

## Challenges and blockers

- The plugin's WebView has no bridge by design, so there is no direct "close"
  call from server content. The navigation event is asynchronous and only fires
  after the landing page loads; the dedicated no-JS route keeps that latency to
  a single tiny response.
- A login round-trip can lose top-level query parameters. The SPA stores the
  token in `sessionStorage`; because storage is per origin and the shell also
  checks the exact origin, a token cannot be replayed against another server.
- The scoped `repoos check` skipped its `tests` step because a remote validation
  runner owned the suite (`REPOOS_SKIP_TESTS=1`). I ran the affected Vitest files
  directly with the repo config (`src/ui-app/vite.config.ts`) — 49 tests pass.
  Running them without that config drops the jsdom environment and produces
  false `localStorage` failures, which is a harness detail, not a product bug.
- I did not run an APK or iOS Simulator build; no real phone was available.
  Contract and source-wiring tests cover the shell logic, but the final
  Android/iOS WebView behaviour needs hardware verification during review. The
  web UI and mobile `www` bundles were both rebuilt.

## Key learnings

- The isolated WebView can still participate in a safe native UX through a
  narrow navigation contract: make the message origin-scoped, path-scoped and
  per-open keyed, and limit the action to dismissing the browser rather than
  exposing any native operation.
- A "return" affordance must be a full document navigation. A Vue route change
  is invisible to a native WebView navigation delegate.
- Keep the contract in a dependency-free core module. The server, the SPA and
  the Capacitor client all need the same constants and decision function;
  duplicating them is how token formats and paths drift.
- Phone top bars are a zero-sum layout. The project name was not hidden for
  style reasons; it competed with a search pill that could flex to fill the row.
  Making search an icon is what creates room for the name.
- Static CSS tests are useful for touch-target/ellipsis guarantees, but they do
  not replace a device check of the actual WebView close; state that boundary
  plainly.
